As a kingdom, Israel shall perish as if it never was in covenant with Him: but as individuals the house of Jacob shall not utterly perish, nay, not one of the least of the righteous shall fall, but only all the sinners (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.7-Amos.9.10">Am 9:7-10</reference>). Restoration of the Jews finally to their own land after the re-establishment of the fallen tabernacle of David; consequent conversion of all the heathen (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11-Amos.9.15">Am 9:11-15</reference>).<div eID="gen23318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23319" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12633"/><hi type="bold">1. This view harmonizes with the similarity of the vision in Amos to that in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Is 6:1-13</reference>, at Jerusalem. Also with the end of this chapter (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11-Amos.9.15">Am 9:11-15</reference>), which applies both to Judah and Israel: "the tabernacle of David," namely, at Jerusalem. entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 9 Am 9:1-15 . Fifth and Last Vision. None can escape the coming judgment in any hiding-place: for God is omnipresent and irresistible ( Am 9:1-6 ). As a kingdom, Israel shall perish as if it never was in covenant with Him: but as individuals the house of Jacob shall not utterly perish, nay, not one of the least of the righteous shall fall, but only all the sinners ( Am 9:7-10 ). Restoration of the Jews finally to their own land after the re-establishment of the fallen tabernacle of David; consequent conversion of all the heathen ( Am 9:11-15 ). 1. Lord ... upon the altar-- namely, in the idolatrous temple at Beth-el; the calves which were spoken of in Am 8:14 . Hither they would flee for protection from the Assyrians, and would perish in the ruins, with the vain object of their trust [Henderson]. Jehovah stands here to direct the destruction of it, them, and the idolatrous nation. He demands many victims on the altar, but they are to be human victims. Calvin and Fairbairn, and others, make it in the temple at Jerusalem. Judgment was to descend both on Israel and Judah. As the services of both alike ought to have been offered on the Jerusalem temple-altar, it is there that Jehovah ideally stands, as if the whole people were assembled there, their abominations lying unpardoned there, and crying for vengeance, though in fact committed elsewhere (compare Eze 8:1-18 ). This view harmonizes with the similarity of the vision in Amos to that in Is 6:1-13 , at Jerusalem. Also with the end of this chapter ( Am 9:11-15 ), which applies both to Judah and Israel: "the tabernacle of David," namely, at Jerusalem. His attitude, "standing," implies fixity of purpose. lintel-- rather, the sphere-like capital of the column [Maurer]. posts-- rather, "thresholds," as in Is 6:4 , Margin. The temple is to be smitten below as well as above, to ensure utter destruction. cut them in the head-- namely, with the broken fragments of the capitals and columns (compare Psa 68:21 ; Ha 3:13 ). slay the last of them-- their posterity [Henderson]. The survivors [Maurer]. Jehovah's directions are addressed to His angels, ministers of judgment (compare Eze 9:1-11 ). he that fleeth ... shall not flee away-- He who fancies himself safe and out of reach of the enemy shall be taken ( Am 2:14 ).

As Amos had threatened that nowhere should the Israelites be safe from the divine judgments, he here shows God's omnipotent ability to execute His threats. So in the case of the threat in <reference osisRef="Amos.8.8">Am 8:8</reference>, God is here stated to be the first cause of the mourning of "all that dwell" in the land, and of its rising "like a flood, and of its being "drowned, as by the flood of Egypt." <div eID="gen23331" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12638"/><div sID="gen23332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12638"/><hi type="bold">6. stories--</hi>literally, "ascents," that is, upper chambers, to which the ascent is by steps [Maurer]; evidently referring to the words in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.13">13</reference>. Grotius explains it, God's royal throne, expressed in language drawn from Solomon's throne, to which the ascent was by steps (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.18">1Ki 10:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.19">19</reference>).<div eID="gen23332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">founded his troop--</hi>namely, all animate creatures, which are God's troop, or host (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.1">Ge 2:1</reference>), doing His will (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.20">Psa 103:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.11">Joe 2:11</reference>). Maurer translates, "His vault," that is, the vaulted sky, which seems to rest on the earth supported by the horizon. <div eID="gen23333" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12639"/><div sID="gen23334" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12639"/><hi type="bold">7. unto me--</hi>however great ye seem to yourselves. Do not rely on past privileges, and on My having delivered you from Egypt, as if therefore I never would remove you from Canaan. I make no more account of you than of "the Ethiopian" (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.13.23">Jr 13:23</reference>). "Have not I (who) brought you out of Egypt," done as much for other peoples? For instance, did I not bring "the Philistines (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.14.29">Is 14:29</reference>, &c.) from Caphtor (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.2.23">De 2:23</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Jer.47.4">Jr 47:4</reference>), where they had been bond-servants, and the Syrians from Kir?" It is appropriate, that as the Syrians migrated into Syria from Kir (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>), so they should be carried back captive into the same land (see on <reference osisRef="Amos.1.15">Am 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 16:9</reference>), just as elsewhere Israel is threatened with a return to Egypt whence they had been delivered. The "Ethiopians," Hebrew, "Cushites," were originally akin to the race that founded Babylon: the cuneiform inscriptions in this confirming independently the Scripture statement (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Ge 10:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.10">8, 10</reference>). <div eID="gen23334" type="x-p"/>

For instance, did I not bring "the Philistines (see on Is 14:29 , &c.) from Caphtor (compare De 2:23 ; see on Jr 47:4 ), where they had been bond-servants, and the Syrians from Kir?" It is appropriate, that as the Syrians migrated into Syria from Kir (compare Note, see on Is 22:6 ), so they should be carried back captive into the same land (see on Am 1:15 ; 2Ki 16:9 ), just as elsewhere Israel is threatened with a return to Egypt whence they had been delivered. The "Ethiopians," Hebrew, "Cushites," were originally akin to the race that founded Babylon: the cuneiform inscriptions in this confirming independently the Scripture statement ( Ge 10:6 , 8, 10 ).

In that day--</hi>quoted by James (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.16">Ac 15:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.17">17</reference>), "After this," that is, in the dispensation of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Ho 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joe 2:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen23340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23341" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tabernacle of David--</hi>not "the house of David," which is used of his affairs when prospering (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.1">2Sa 3:1</reference>), but the tent or booth, expressing the low condition to which his kingdom and family had fallen in Amos' time, and subsequently at the Babylonian captivity before the restoration; and secondarily, in the last days preceding Israel's restoration under Messiah, the antitype to David (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.13">Psa 102:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jr 30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">Eze 34:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.24">37:24</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Is 12:1</reference>). The type is taken from architecture (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>). The restoration under Zerubbabel can only be a partial, temporary fulfilment; for it did not include Israel, which nation is the main subject of Amos' prophecies, but only Judah; also Zerubbabel's kingdom was not independent and settled; also all the prophets end their prophecies with Messiah, whose advent is the cure of all previous disorders. "Tabernacle" is appropriate to Him, as His human nature is the tabernacle which He assumed in becoming Immanuel, "God with us" (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>). "Dwelt," literally, tabernacled "among us" (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Re 21:3</reference>). Some understand "the tabernacle of David" as that which David pitched for the ark in Zion, after bringing it from Obed-edom's house. It remained there all his reign for thirty years, till the temple of Solomon was built, whereas the "tabernacle of the congregation" remained at Gibeon (<reference osisRef="2Chr.1.3">2Ch 1:3</reference>), where the priests ministered in sacrifices (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.39">1Ch 16:39</reference>). Song and praise was the service of David's attendants before the ark (Asaph, &c.): a type of the gospel separation between the sacrificial service (Messiah's priesthood now in heaven) and the access of believers on earth to the presence of God, apart from the former (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.12-2Sam.6.17">2Sa 6:12-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.37-1Chr.16.39">1Ch 16:37-39</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.3">2Ch 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen23341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breaches thereof--</hi>literally, "of them," that is, of the whole nation, Israel as well as Judah.<div eID="gen23342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as in ... days of old--</hi>as it was formerly in the days of David and Solomon, when the kingdom was in its full extent and undivided. <div eID="gen23343" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12644"/><div sID="gen23344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12644"/><hi type="bold">12. That they may possess ... remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen--</hi>"Edom," the bitter foe, though the brother, of Israel; therefore to be punished (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">Am 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>), Israel shall be lord of the "remnant" of Edom left after the punishment of the latter. James quotes it, "That the residue of men might seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles," &c. For "all the heathen" nations stand on the same footing as Edom: Edom is the representative of them all. The residue or remnant in both cases expresses those left after great antecedent calamities (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.27">Ro 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>). Here the conversion of "all nations" (of which the earnest was given in James's time) is represented as only to be realized on the re-establishment of the theocracy under Messiah, the Heir of the throne of David (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Am 9:11</reference>). The possession of the heathen nations by Israel is to be spiritual, the latter being the ministers to the former for their conversion to Messiah, King of the Jews; just as the first conversions of pagans were through the ministry of the apostles, who were Jews. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.54.3">Is 54:3</reference>, "thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">Is 49:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.13">Ro 4:13</reference>). A remnant of Edom became Jews under John Hyrcanus, and the rest amalgamated with the Arabians, who became Christians subsequently.<div eID="gen23344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23345" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which are called by my name--</hi>that is, who belong to Me, whom I claim as Mine (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Psa 2:8</reference>); in the purposes of electing grace, God terms them already called by His name. Compare the title, "the children," applied by anticipation, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>. Hence as an act of sovereign grace, fulfilling His promise, it is spoken of God. Proclaim His title as sovereign, "the Lord that doeth this" ("all these things," <reference osisRef="Acts.15.17">Ac 15:17</reference>, namely, all these and such like acts of sovereign love). <div eID="gen23345" type="x-p"/>
